european_mantis_two_jobs.title: THE MANTIS THAT USES ITS ARMS TWICE
european_mantis_two_jobs.script: Why is this European mantis holding its spiky front legs so high? Those folded legs are built to grip, with rows of sharp spines along the inside. When another insect gets close, the mantis snaps forward and traps it between those spines. The grip keeps struggling prey from escaping while the mantis begins to feed. But raised arms can also be a warning display when the mantis feels threatened. The same pair of legs can catch a meal or make a much larger enemy think twice.
european_mantis_two_jobs.caption: THE MANTIS THAT USES ITS ARMS TWICE. #WildVox #Wildlife #Nature #AnimalFacts

common_kingfisher_nest_tunnel.title: WHY A KINGFISHER DIGS INTO A RIVERBANK
common_kingfisher_nest_tunnel.script: This common kingfisher is digging into a riverbank instead of diving for fish. Near the water, a safe nesting place matters as much as finding the next meal. It visits the narrow opening again and again, working toward a sheltered chamber. The tunnel puts eggs and young chicks away from the exposed surface of the bank. That pointed bill is also a fishing tool, used to handle slippery prey. One little bird uses the same bill to prepare a home and to bring food back.
common_kingfisher_nest_tunnel.caption: WHY A KINGFISHER DIGS INTO A RIVERBANK. #WildVox #Wildlife #Nature #AnimalFacts

bald_eagle_feeding_eaglets.title: THE PATIENT SIDE OF A BALD EAGLE
bald_eagle_feeding_eaglets.script: A bald eagle is feeding tiny chicks, even though its own beak can tear apart a large fish. Young eaglets cannot hunt yet, so the adults must bring food back to the nest. Watch how a parent offers small bites instead of leaving the whole catch to the chicks. The chicks grow for weeks before they can fly or find food on their own. Even powerful adults face trouble: smaller birds sometimes chase them away from nesting areas. Behind the fierce predator is a long period of care before a young eagle can hunt.
bald_eagle_feeding_eaglets.caption: THE PATIENT SIDE OF A BALD EAGLE. #WildVox #Wildlife #Nature #AnimalFacts

north_american_beaver_water_design.title: WHY BEAVERS MOVE BETTER IN WATER
north_american_beaver_water_design.script: A North American beaver looks heavy on land, but its body is made for a life near water. Broad hind feet and a flat tail help this rodent maneuver through ponds. When it swims, the hind feet do most of the paddling and the tail helps it steer. Its thick fur helps trap warmth, while regular grooming keeps that coat working. That same bulky animal can turn smoothly once its body is supported by water. For a beaver, the boundary between land and water is where its special body design pays off.
north_american_beaver_water_design.caption: WHY BEAVERS MOVE BETTER IN WATER. #WildVox #Wildlife #Nature #AnimalFacts

american_alligator_hidden_breath.title: THE ALLIGATOR YOU CAN BARELY SEE
american_alligator_hidden_breath.script: An American alligator can seem to vanish with only its eyes showing above the water. Its eyes and nostrils sit high on the head, while the heavy body stays low. A slow sweep of the tail can move the animal through water with little splash. Inside, strong muscles move air through its lungs, something scientists can study with X-ray video. An albino alligator stands out, but its eyes and nostrils keep the same basic arrangement. Dark or pale, the same body plan helps an alligator watch the world from the waterline.
american_alligator_hidden_breath.caption: THE ALLIGATOR YOU CAN BARELY SEE. #WildVox #Wildlife #Nature #AnimalFacts
